source.title: Evaluating Neuron Explanations: A Unified Framework with Sanity Checks
source.authors: Tuomas P. Oikarinen; Ge Yan; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether evaluation metrics can distinguish a correct neuron concept from an overly generic one, and finds that Recall often cannot. This refines the claim that fitting highly activating examples establishes what a neuron does.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates explanation-scoring metrics, not the prevalence of interpretable neurons or the quality of explanations produced by stronger explainer models. Results cited from other studies are not extracted as rows. Only results directly relevant to whether highly activating examples can conceal overly generic explanations are included.
record.test_reason: The paper shows that scoring an explanation only on highly activating inputs (Recall, which it shows equals crowdsourced top-example rating) cannot tell a correct concept from an overly generic superset. This is V6's mechanism: an explanation can fit activating examples yet mispredict where the neuron fires. It is tested in a toy example, on idealized neurons and on real vision and GPT-2 neurons with perturbed ground-truth labels. It does not measure how often real generated explanations are over-generic.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that neuron explanation evaluations should use metrics passing both the Missing and Extra Labels tests, and name Correlation, Cosine, AUPRC, F1 and IoU as passing. Recall (top-activating-only evaluation), AUC, MAD and top-and-random sampling fail and should not be relied on alone. Correlation, Cosine and AUPRC performed best on neurons with known concepts.
record.recipe_differences: The study meta-evaluates explanation-scoring metrics with label perturbation tests and known-concept comparisons; it does not generate neuron explanations or replicate the original audit.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that top-and-random sampling changes Correlation's behavior: it fails the Extra Labels Test, unlike Correlation with uniform sampling.

fits_no_version.finding: Bills-style simulation scoring with top-and-random sampling (Correlation T&R) fails the extra-labels test: 60.26% experimental and 43.64% theoretical Decrease Acc. It is thus biased toward over-generic explanations. The authors link this to Huang et al. finding high T&R scores alongside low F1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-and-random simulation scores can overrate overly generic neuron explanations, so automated simulation scores may overstate explanation quality.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: For the V6-relevant evidence, some tests use hypothetical or synthetically altered concept labels rather than auditing naturally generated neuron explanations. The aggregate experimental results combine multiple settings, and the paper does not report uncertainty intervals for these results.
record.rows_left_out: Other metric results in Tables 3, 4, and the appendices were omitted because they do not specifically test whether highly activating examples can conceal an overly generic concept. Results about cited prior studies were not extracted.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or interpretability shares.
No interpretability shares across models or scale.
No analysis of InceptionV1 canonical polysemantic neurons.
No test of architecture or tools as causes, and no interpretable-neuron share estimates.

How often real, naturally generated explanations judged from activating examples are over-generic, and by how much inspection overstates what is explained, are not measured. Only metric behaviour under synthetic or WordNet label perturbations is tested.
No fraction of neurons with good simulation scores, and no comparison of explainer models.

missing.what: Per-setting Recall extra-labels Decrease Acc of 0.00% in all 8 settings, including GPT-2-small and GPT-2-XL final-layer neurons, ResNet layer4 hidden neurons, a CBM and a CLIP probe.
Correlation(T&R) extra-labels failure: 60.26% experimental and 43.64% theoretical Decrease Acc.
Meta-AUPRC on neurons with known concepts: Recall avg 0.6722, rank 11.3 of 17, worst in the CUB CBM setting (0.3958). This shows Recall discriminates correct explanations poorly.

record.verdict_notes: Recall's failure on the extra-labels test holds by construction: adding positive labels cannot lower it (eq. D.2). The rows therefore show a property of the scoring method, demonstrated on real neurons, not an empirical rate of over-generic explanations. The original record's 'absent' states were inverted relative to V6. Rows r7 and r8 misread Table E.3: the superclass neurons were used only for the missing-labels test.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole-level shares are not measured.
The study does not estimate interpretability shares across models or scale.
The study does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons or recursive generalization.
The study does not test architectural causes or estimates of interpretable-neuron shares.
Attribution graphs and neuron-based circuit reconstruction are not evaluated.

The study tests whether Recall-based evaluation can distinguish correct concepts from overly generic ones, but does not directly audit explanations generated from activating examples or quantify how much of a neuron's behavior is explained.
The study does not measure the fraction of neurons receiving good explanation-simulation scores, nor compare stronger explainer models on that outcome.

rows.subject: hypothetical pet neuron
rows.operation_detail: Scored dog as an explanation with Recall in the illustrative pet-neuron example.
rows.note: The paper presents this as a hypothetical neuron that activates on pets; the score alone does not establish whether this explanation predicts activation on all inputs.
rows.check: 'dog' is a too-specific concept. A lower Recall for it bears on the missing-labels failure, not V6. Illustrative toy value only.

rows.subject: hypothetical pet neuron

labels.condition: Evaluation restricted to highly activating inputs (Recall): toy pet example, idealized neurons, and real vision/GPT-2 neurons with random or WordNet-superset labels
labels.reason: Recall scores animal equal to pet (r4) and has 0.00% Decrease Acc in every extra-labels setting (r5, r6, r9, r10). The over-generic labels are constructed, and WordNet supersets were run on ViT-B-16 only.

relation.reason: Its own results (Tables 2, 3, E.3) bear on V6's mechanism: top-example scoring can't tell when an explanation fits activating inputs but over-predicts firing.

tranche.reason: The study gives results and a specific argument that judging explanations only on highly activating inputs (Recall, equal to crowdsourced top-example rating) cannot catch over-generic explanations. App. B.4 attributes interpretability illusions to this. That is the challenge V6 states, so T5 fits.

source_check.notes: Every over-generic label is constructed: a toy example, random supersets of ground-truth labels, or WordNet superclasses (ViT-B-16 only). No generated explanations are scored, and the paper does not measure how much inspection overstates. In l0's condition, 'WordNet-superset' applies only to ViT-B-16. GPT-2 appears only in the 8-setting random-superset average.
